newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan thanks Peru,Cuba,Canada, starts victims fund.
newsitem.headline: Japan thanks Peru,Cuba,Canada, starts victims fund.

text.p: Japan thanked Peru again on Thursday for resolving the hostage crisis in Lima and also expressed gratitude to Canada and Cuba for their help in the four-month affair.
Japan's parliament adopted a resolution thanking Peru while Japanese volunteers started a private fund for the families of the hostage and two soldiers who died in the commando raid, officials said.

"I would like to thank Peru from the bottom of my heart for thoroughly preparing for the raid and successfully freeing most of the hostages," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told a plenary session of the Lower House of parliament.
"We aim to combat terrorism in cooperation with the international community," Hashimoto added.
Hashimoto also thanked Canada and Cuba for their help.
"We were helped by Canada, especially by Canadian ambassador Vincent to the very end of the affair," Hashimoto told Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on the telephone.
Ambassador Anthony Vincent, originally a hostage himself, was one of three members of a top mediators' group which was trying to achieve a bloodless end to the crisis.

Peruvian commandos stormed the Lima residence of the Japanese ambassador on Tuesday and freed all but one of the 72 hostages. Besides the hostage and two commandos who died, all of the 14 Marxist rebels were killed in the raid.
"We are glad it ended with a minimal loss of life," Hashimoto told Chretien.
Hashimoto was also preparing to send a letter of thanks to Cuban President Fidel Castro, government sources said.
Cuba said it would have taken in the Marxist rebels if they had agreed on a deal to release the hostages in exchange for safe passage to a foreign country.

Hisahiko Okazaki, a retired diplomat and former ambassador to Thailand, said he and other volunteers will start asking for donations to set up a private fund for the families of the hostage and two soldiers who died in the raid, Foreign Ministry officials said.

Japanese newspapers on Thursday said Japan's own record of going soft against terrorism in general may have brought about the crisis and urged the government to help Peru combat poverty, the root cause of leftist insurgencies.

"Perhaps the MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement) side had this optimistic notion that Japan, which persistently demanded a peaceful resolution, would prevent Peru from storming the residence," said the Yomiuri Shimbun, Japan's largest circulation daily.
"Japan should adopt a stiff attitude against terrorism to get rid of such an image," the Yomiuri said in an editorial.
The Tokyo Shimbun said the world focused on Japan's behaviour in the crisis because of suspicions that Tokyo may once again give in to guerrilla demands.

"The world began to focus its attention on Japan because in the past, our country gave in to terrorists without principle, having put too much weight on saving the lives of hostages," the Tokyo Shimbun editorial said.
The Asahi Shimbun said Japan should use its foreign aid to help Peru contain poverty.

"The case brought reports of unimaginable poverty to living rooms (in Japan)," the Asahi Shimbun editorial said. "We must study if Japan was really using its ODA (foreign aid) to the benefit of the people."
